problem: The sentence 'the loop oscillates when the total phase is 180° plus inversion' is muddled: it never states the total needed (360°) and 'plus inversion' is unclear to a first-time reader, who may think 180° alone is the condition.
fix: Say: an odd number of inverting stages gives 180° of phase shift from the inversion alone; each stage also adds delay, and the loop oscillates at the frequency where the stages add a further 180°, making the total loop phase 360° (or a multiple of it).

problem: The plotted slopes do not match the Leeson slopes taught in the same section. VCO falls 20 dB from 1 kHz to 10 kHz but only 10 dB per decade from 10 kHz to 1 MHz, and the reference path also has 10 dB/decade segments. The text states the regions are 30 dB/decade (1/f³) and 20 dB/decade (1/f²), so a student sees a 10 dB/decade slope that the model does not predict.
fix: Keep the 1 MHz values where they are and make the intermediate points follow the taught slopes, e.g. VCO: 1 kHz −60, 10 kHz −80, 100 kHz −100, 1 MHz −105 (20 dB/decade, then flattening to a floor); reference path: 1 kHz −110, 10 kHz −130, 100 kHz −150 with a floor near −150 to −155.

problem: 'The 20 comes from voltage; 10 would be a power ratio without squaring' does not explain why a power-like quantity gives 20 log N, and can leave the student confused about why phase noise, measured in dBc, scales by 20.
fix: Say: multiplication by N multiplies the phase deviation by N, so the phase-noise power (variance of phase) scales by N², and in dB that is 10 log₁₀(N²) = 20 log₁₀N.
